name: Kimura Sweep
summary: The Kimura Sweep is a Closed Guard reversal that traps the opponent's arm in a figure-four grip and uses it as a lever to roll them over into Mount, forcing a sweep-or-submit dilemma.
description: Master the Kimura Sweep in BJJ. Execute from Closed Guard to Mount using figure-four grip mechanics. Complete guide with attacker and defender perspectives.
overview:
The Kimura Sweep is a powerful positional advancement technique that leverages the figure-four grip control to off-balance and sweep the opponent from Closed Guard directly to Mount. This sweep capitalizes on the mechanical advantage created when you secure the Kimura grip on the opponent's arm, using their trapped limb as a lever to disrupt their base and facilitate the reversal. The technique represents a fundamental concept in guard work where grip fighting transitions directly into sweeping opportunities rather than remaining as isolated submission attempts.

Strategically, the Kimura Sweep creates a dilemma for the opponent: defend the Kimura grip and become vulnerable to the sweep, or post their hand to maintain base and risk the submission. This attack-sweep duality makes the Kimura grip one of the most versatile tools from Closed Guard. The sweep works particularly well against opponents who attempt to posture up or establish a strong base, as their weight distribution makes them susceptible to being rolled.

At higher levels, the Kimura Sweep integrates into broader attacking systems where the initial grip threat forces reactions that open pathways to back takes, hip bumps, or direct submission finishes. Understanding when to commit to the sweep versus when to maintain grip pressure for other attacks distinguishes intermediate from advanced practitioners.
conditions: Closed Guard must be established with ankles locked behind opponent
Opponent's posture must be broken or breakable to allow wrist access
Sufficient hip mobility to create angle for the sweep direction
Opponent has at least one arm within reach for Kimura grip capture

attacker.name: Kimura Sweep Attacker
attacker.description: How to execute Kimura Sweep in BJJ. Attacking perspective with setup, execution steps, and counters from Closed Guard to Mount.
attacker.overview:
The Kimura Sweep is a powerful positional advancement technique that leverages the figure-four grip control to off-balance and sweep the opponent from Closed Guard directly to Mount. This sweep capitalizes on the mechanical advantage created when you secure the Kimura grip on the opponent's arm, using their trapped limb as a lever to disrupt their base and facilitate the reversal. The technique represents a fundamental concept in guard work where grip fighting transitions directly into sweeping opportunities rather than remaining as isolated submission attempts.

Strategically, the Kimura Sweep creates a dilemma for the opponent: defend the Kimura grip and become vulnerable to the sweep, or post their hand to maintain base and risk the submission. This attack-sweep duality makes the Kimura grip one of the most versatile tools from Closed Guard. The sweep works particularly well against opponents who attempt to posture up or establish a strong base, as their weight distribution makes them susceptible to being rolled.

At higher levels, the Kimura Sweep integrates into broader attacking systems where the initial grip threat forces reactions that open pathways to back takes, hip bumps, or direct submission finishes. Understanding when to commit to the sweep versus when to maintain grip pressure for other attacks distinguishes intermediate from advanced practitioners.
key_principles: Secure the figure-four grip before attempting any sweep motion to ensure mechanical control
Break opponent's posture first by pulling their elbow across your centerline
Use hip escape to create the angle necessary for leverage against opponent's base
Time the sweep when opponent posts their hand or shifts weight backward
Maintain tight elbow connection throughout the sweep to prevent grip breaks
Drive through the shoulder rather than pulling with arms alone for sweep power
Follow through immediately to secure Mount before opponent can recover base
setup_requirements: Closed Guard established with opponent inside your leg triangle
Figure-four Kimura grip secured on opponent's wrist and elbow
Opponent's posture broken with their chest relatively close to yours
Hip escape angle created to load weight onto one hip for leverage
Opponent's trapped arm isolated across your body centerline

execution_steps.description: From Closed Guard, control opponent's wrist with your same-side hand while threading your opposite arm under their tricep to grab your own wrist, creating the figure-four lock. Ensure your grip hand wraps fully around your own wrist for maximum security.

Pull opponent's trapped elbow across your centerline while using your legs to break their posture forward, bringing their weight over your body. The arm should be drawn tight against your chest so there is no slack in the lever system.

Hip escape to the side opposite the trapped arm, loading your weight onto one hip while maintaining the Kimura grip tight to your chest. This angular displacement is the key mechanical element that converts your hip drive into rotational force against their base.

Unlock your ankles and place your foot flat on the mat on the side you hip escaped toward, keeping the opposite leg as a hook across opponent's hip. The posted foot becomes your primary driving platform for generating sweep power.

Drive through opponent's shoulder using the Kimura grip as a steering wheel while simultaneously pushing off your posted foot and pulling with your hook leg. The force vectors should converge to roll the opponent over the shoulder of the trapped arm.

Commit your body weight forward and over the opponent as they roll, staying chest-to-chest throughout the transition. Do not release the Kimura grip or allow any space between your torso and their body during the rolling motion.

As you land on top, immediately widen your knees to establish base in Mount position while maintaining the Kimura grip on the trapped arm. Settle your hips low onto their torso before deciding whether to maintain the grip for continued attacks or release to establish standard Mount control.

common_counters.counter: Opponent straightens trapped arm to break grip connection
common_counters.your_response: Transition to straight armlock on the extended arm, or use their focus on the arm to switch to hip bump sweep while their base is compromised

common_counters.counter: Opponent drops weight and flattens to prevent the roll
common_counters.your_response: Abandon sweep and attack with Kimura submission directly since their flat position exposes the shoulder, or transition to back take as they turn

common_counters.counter: Opponent posts free hand wide to maintain base during sweep attempt
common_counters.your_response: Use the posting hand as opportunity for armbar setup on the extended arm, or increase hip drive explosiveness to power through their weakened base

common_counters.counter: Opponent stacks forward into your guard to nullify hip escape angle
common_counters.your_response: Switch to pendulum sweep or elevator sweep using their forward momentum against them, or retain guard and reset the attack sequence

common_counters.counter: Opponent strips wrist grip by pulling elbow sharply back before figure-four locks
common_counters.your_response: Immediately transition to overhook control on the same arm to maintain upper body connection, then reattempt Kimura grip or switch to triangle setup

common_errors.error: Attempting sweep without breaking opponent's posture first
common_errors.consequence: Opponent maintains strong base and easily resists the sweep, potentially passing your guard
common_errors.correction: Always pull opponent's elbow across centerline and use legs to break posture before initiating sweep motion

common_errors.error: Keeping guard closed during sweep attempt
common_errors.consequence: Unable to generate hip movement and angle necessary for leverage, sweep stalls
common_errors.correction: Open guard deliberately, post one foot on mat, and use other leg as active hook to assist sweep

common_errors.error: Holding Kimura grip too far from body during sweep
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can straighten arm and break grip, losing control entirely
common_errors.correction: Keep trapped arm pinned tight to your chest throughout entire sweep sequence

common_errors.error: Pulling with arms instead of driving through hips
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient power to complete sweep, rapid arm fatigue, grip failure
common_errors.correction: Focus on hip drive and leg engagement as primary sweep power, arms maintain grip only

common_errors.error: Failing to follow through to Mount after successful sweep
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recovers half guard or full guard, negating positional advantage gained
common_errors.correction: Immediately advance to Mount as sweep completes, maintaining arm control throughout transition

common_errors.error: Hip escaping to the same side as the trapped arm
common_errors.consequence: Creates angle that works against the sweep direction, eliminating rotational leverage
common_errors.correction: Always hip escape to the side opposite the trapped arm so your body weight loads in the correct direction for the roll

training_progressions.description: Practice securing the figure-four Kimura grip from Closed Guard against a stationary partner. Focus on proper wrist positioning, elbow threading, and keeping the grip tight to chest. Drill grip acquisition 50 times per session.

Add the hip escape and sweep motion with compliant partner. Focus on timing the guard opening, foot posting, and hip drive. Partner allows sweep completion to build muscle memory for the full sequence.
Partner provides moderate resistance and common defensive reactions. Practice recognizing when to commit to sweep versus transition to submission. Introduce chain attacks when sweep is defended.

Drill the full decision tree: hip bump to Kimura grip, sweep attempt to submission switch, and back take option when opponent turns. Build automatic recognition of which path to take based on opponent reaction.

Apply Kimura Sweep in positional sparring starting from Closed Guard. Work on setting up the grip naturally during live rolls and recognizing optimal sweep timing against fully resisting opponents at competition pace.

flashcards.question: What is the primary mechanical advantage that makes the Kimura Sweep effective?
flashcards.answer: The figure-four grip forms a lever that lets your whole arm strength control the opponent's shoulder and disrupt their base. Because their limb is trapped in this lever system, your hip drive translates directly into the rotational force needed for the sweep, turning their own arm into the handle that tips them over.

flashcards.question: Why must you hip escape before attempting the sweep motion?
flashcards.answer: The hip escape creates the angular leverage necessary to load your weight onto one hip, which generates the rotational force to roll the opponent. Without the angle, you're pushing directly into their base rather than around it.

flashcards.question: Your opponent straightens their trapped arm when you secure the Kimura grip. How do you adjust?
flashcards.answer: Attack a straight armlock on the extended arm, or switch to a hip bump sweep while their attention is on defending the arm. The straightened arm hands you a new submission threat, and their focus on grip-fighting means their base maintenance is neglected — exactly the moment a sweep succeeds.

flashcards.question: What distinguishes when to finish the Kimura submission versus executing the sweep?
flashcards.answer: Finish the submission when opponent's weight drops and they flatten to defend. Execute the sweep when opponent maintains posture or shifts weight backward to create base, as this weight distribution makes them vulnerable to being rolled.
flashcards.answer_line: Finish if flat, sweep if based

plausible: Finish sub as soon as secured

flashcards.question: Why is it critical to keep the trapped arm pinned to your chest throughout the sweep?
flashcards.answer: Pinning the arm to your chest stops them straightening to break the grip and keeps the lever intact so hip drive becomes rotation. This preserves your mechanical advantage for the whole movement, ensuring the force you generate transfers directly into turning their body rather than leaking out through a loose connection.

plausible: Only pin arm at the start

flashcards.question: Your opponent posts their free hand wide to resist the sweep. How do you capitalize on this?
flashcards.answer: The wide post exposes that extended arm to an armbar, or you can drive your hips harder through their now wider, weaker base. A hand posted far from their center spreads their weight across a less stable platform, so either attack the offered arm or add explosive hip drive to power through the compromised structure.
flashcards.answer_line: Attack posted arm or drive hips

flashcards.question: What leg positioning optimizes the sweep power during execution?
flashcards.answer: Post the foot on the side you are hip escaping toward, and keep the opposite leg as an active hook on the opponent's hip. The posted foot gives you driving power off the mat, while the hook pulls them into the rotation and prevents them from stepping around to recover their base.
flashcards.answer_line: Post near foot, hook far hip

flashcards.question: How does the Kimura Sweep integrate with the hip bump sweep as a combination attack?
flashcards.answer: Attempt hip bump first to force opponent to post their hand for base. The posting hand becomes the target for Kimura grip, and the sweep executes in the opposite direction from the hip bump, catching opponent in transition between defensive positions.

flashcards.question: What is the optimal timing window for initiating the sweep once the Kimura grip is secured?
flashcards.answer: The optimal window is immediately after breaking posture and completing the hip escape to angle, before the opponent has time to establish a defensive base. Hesitation allows them to widen their knees, post a hand, or begin stripping your grip.

flashcards.question: Your opponent stacks forward aggressively to nullify your hip escape angle. What chain attack do you pursue?
flashcards.answer: Use their forward momentum against them by switching to a pendulum sweep or elevator sweep. Their committed forward weight shift eliminates their ability to post backward, making them highly vulnerable to sweeps that redirect their momentum over your head or to the side.

attacker.safety_considerations: The Kimura Sweep is relatively low-risk compared to submission techniques, but attention to shoulder safety remains important. During drilling, avoid cranking the Kimura grip aggressively as the sweep completes, as landing momentum can add unexpected force to the shoulder joint. Partners should tap immediately if shoulder pressure becomes uncomfortable during sweep practice. When learning, focus on smooth technique rather than explosive power to prevent accidental joint strain. Avoid this sweep if you have existing wrist or elbow injuries, as the gripping demands can aggravate these conditions.

defender.name: Kimura Sweep Defender
defender.description: How to defend against Kimura Sweep in BJJ. Recognition cues, defensive options, and escape strategies from the top player's perspective inside Closed Guard.
defender.overview:
Defending the Kimura Sweep requires the top player to recognize the attack early and address both the grip threat and the sweep mechanics simultaneously. As the player inside Closed Guard, you must understand that the Kimura grip creates a dual threat: the sweep itself and the submission. Your defensive priority is to prevent the figure-four grip from being consolidated, and if it is secured, to deny the angular leverage your opponent needs to execute the roll. The most common defensive failure is treating the grip and the sweep as separate problems rather than understanding they work as a unified system.

Effective defense begins with posture and hand positioning. Keeping your elbows tight and your hands connected to your opponent's hips or biceps denies them easy access to your wrist for the initial grip capture. Once the grip is established, your defensive window narrows significantly, and you must act decisively: either strip the grip immediately or flatten your weight to deny the hip escape angle that makes the sweep mechanically possible.

At higher levels, skilled defenders learn to use the opponent's commitment to the Kimura grip as an opening for guard passing. When the bottom player invests in maintaining the grip, they often compromise their guard closure and hip positioning, creating passing opportunities that would not exist against a neutral guard player.
key_principles: Maintain strong posture with elbows tucked tight to deny wrist access for the initial Kimura grip capture
Recognize the grip threat early and strip it before the figure-four is fully consolidated around your wrist
Keep your weight centered and base wide to resist the rotational force generated by the sweep
Drive your trapped elbow back toward your own hip rather than fighting the grip with arm extension
Flatten your weight forward when the grip is established to deny the hip escape angle needed for sweep leverage
Use the opponent's grip commitment as a guard passing opportunity by driving through their compromised guard structure
recognition_cues: Opponent grabs your wrist with their same-side hand and begins threading their opposite arm under your tricep
Opponent pulls your elbow sharply across their centerline while increasing leg squeeze to break your posture
Opponent hip escapes to one side while maintaining tight grip on your arm, loading their weight onto one hip
Opponent opens their guard and posts one foot on the mat while keeping a hook on your opposite hip

defensive_options.action: Strip the grip early by circling your trapped arm toward your own body and pulling your elbow back sharply to your hip
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when you feel opponent grab your wrist before the figure-four is fully locked
defensive_options.if_successful: Return to standard Closed Guard top position with posture re-established and opponent's attack neutralized
defensive_options.risk: If grip strip fails, opponent tightens the figure-four and you have expended energy without improving position

defensive_options.action: Flatten your weight forward onto opponent's chest while driving your hips down to deny the hip escape angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the Kimura grip is secured and opponent begins hip escaping to create sweep angle
defensive_options.if_successful: Opponent cannot generate the angular leverage needed for the sweep, grip becomes less threatening, and you can work to strip it from the flattened position
defensive_options.risk: Flattening forward exposes you to the Kimura submission itself if opponent abandons sweep and attacks the shoulder directly

defensive_options.action: Post your free hand wide on the mat on the side opponent is trying to sweep you toward, creating a tripod base
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you feel the sweep motion beginning and cannot strip the grip in time
defensive_options.if_successful: Posted hand absorbs sweep momentum and prevents the roll, giving you time to work the grip strip or posture recovery
defensive_options.risk: Extended posting arm becomes a target for armbar, and a strong opponent may power through the post with explosive hip drive

defensive_options.action: Stand up explosively to break the guard and create distance, taking the Kimura grip with you
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you recognize the grip early and still have good base before opponent creates significant angle
defensive_options.if_successful: Standing breaks the guard closure and eliminates the leg hook needed for sweep mechanics, allowing you to strip the grip from a standing position
defensive_options.risk: If opponent maintains grip and pulls you back down, you may land in a worse angle than before the stand attempt

favorable_outcomes.how: Strip the Kimura grip early before the figure-four is consolidated by pulling your elbow sharply back to your hip and circling your wrist free. Re-establish posture with hands on opponent's hips to prevent re-engagement.

If the sweep partially succeeds but you manage to disengage during the roll by posting and scrambling, you may end in a side control position. While not ideal, extracting from the Kimura grip during the scramble prevents the opponent from achieving full mount with arm control.

common_errors.error: Extending the trapped arm straight to try to power out of the Kimura grip
common_errors.consequence: Straightening the arm exposes it to armbar attack and actually makes the grip harder to break since the figure-four controls a straight arm effectively
common_errors.correction: Keep the trapped elbow bent and drive it back toward your own hip using your body rotation rather than arm extension to strip the grip

common_errors.error: Leaning away from the sweep direction to resist the roll
common_errors.consequence: Creates a wider base momentarily but shifts your center of gravity high, making you more susceptible to the rotational force once opponent commits to the drive
common_errors.correction: Drive your weight forward and down into opponent's chest to deny the hip escape angle rather than leaning laterally away from the sweep direction

common_errors.error: Ignoring the grip and attempting to pass guard while the Kimura is still secured
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses your movement to accelerate the sweep since passing attempts shift your base and create the exact angle they need for the roll
common_errors.correction: Address the Kimura grip first before attempting any guard passing. Strip the grip or flatten your weight to neutralize it, then resume passing sequences

common_errors.error: Keeping knees narrow under opponent's guard when the grip is established
common_errors.consequence: Narrow base provides minimal resistance to the lateral rotational force, making the sweep nearly impossible to stop even with good grip defense
common_errors.correction: Widen your knees immediately when you feel the Kimura grip establish, creating a broader base that requires significantly more force to roll

flashcards.question: What is the earliest recognition cue that your opponent is setting up the Kimura Sweep?
flashcards.answer: The earliest cue is feeling your opponent grab your wrist with their same-side hand. This is the entry point for the figure-four grip. Immediately pull your elbow back to your hip and circle your wrist free before they can thread their opposite arm under your tricep to complete the lock.

trap: Let them finish the grip first

flashcards.question: Your opponent has secured the Kimura grip and begins hip escaping. What is your immediate priority?
flashcards.answer: Drive your weight forward and down onto their chest while simultaneously widening your knees for base. This denies the hip escape angle that creates the rotational leverage for the sweep. Do not try to posture up, as this lifts your weight and makes the sweep easier.

trap: Posture up out of the grip

flashcards.question: Why is extending your trapped arm to escape the grip a dangerous mistake?
flashcards.answer: Extending the arm straightens it into a position where your opponent can transition directly to an armbar attack. The figure-four grip controls a straight arm effectively, so extension does not break the grip but instead opens a more dangerous submission threat while weakening your base.

flashcards.question: How can you turn a defended Kimura Sweep into a guard passing opportunity?
flashcards.answer: When your opponent commits both arms to the Kimura grip and opens their guard to create sweep angle, their legs are no longer fully controlling your hips. After neutralizing the sweep by flattening your weight or stripping the grip, immediately drive your hips through the open guard space and work to pass before they can re-close their guard.

flashcards.question: Your opponent opens their guard and posts a foot to begin the sweep drive. What defensive adjustment do you make?
flashcards.answer: Post your free hand on the mat on the side they are sweeping you toward while dropping your hip on the opposite side. The posted hand creates a tripod base absorbing the sweep momentum. Simultaneously, attempt to trap their posted foot with your leg to eliminate their driving platform and collapse the sweep mechanics.

training_progressions.description: Partner attempts to secure Kimura grip from Closed Guard while you practice keeping elbows tight, recognizing wrist control attempts, and executing immediate grip strips. 50 repetitions per session focusing on speed of recognition.

Partner secures the Kimura grip and you practice flattening weight, widening base, and driving your trapped elbow back. Work the defensive posture with partner providing progressive sweep attempts at 30-60% resistance.

After successfully defending the sweep, immediately chain into guard passing attempts through the opened guard. Build the habit of converting defensive success into offensive transitions rather than simply returning to neutral.

Begin from inside opponent's Closed Guard with them targeting the Kimura Sweep. Practice the full defensive sequence against fully resisting partners, including grip prevention, sweep defense, and counter-passing at competition intensity.

variants_and_adaptations.variant_name: Hip Bump to Kimura Sweep Combination
variants_and_adaptations.description: Initiate with hip bump sweep attempt; when opponent posts hand to base, immediately capture that arm in Kimura grip and execute sweep in opposite direction
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against opponents who react quickly to hip bump threats with strong posting

variants_and_adaptations.description: When opponent resists sweep by turning into you, release Mount pursuit and take the back instead, using Kimura grip to control their rotation
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent has strong base but commits to turning to prevent being swept

variants_and_adaptations.description: Secure overhook control before establishing Kimura grip for added security without gi friction, using elbow pit pressure to control opponent's arm
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: In no-gi situations where grip security requires additional control points

position_integration: The Kimura Sweep occupies a central position in the Closed Guard attacking system, serving as the bridge between grip fighting and positional advancement. It connects directly to the Kimura submission when opponents flatten to defend, creating the classic sweep-or-submit dilemma. The sweep chains naturally from hip bump attempts when opponents post to base, and leads to Mount where the Kimura grip can be maintained for continued attacks. Understanding this technique unlocks the broader Closed Guard offensive framework where every grip threatens multiple outcomes, forcing opponents into reactive defense rather than proactive passing.
